title: Rows into columns, columns unknown in advance
prompt:
You are given exam records, each `{ student, subject, score }` — one row per student per subject they sat. Pivot this into one CSV row per student, with one column per subject.

The list of subjects is not given anywhere; it has to be discovered from the data, in the order each subject first appears. If a student has no record for some subject that other students do have, that student's cell for it is `0` — every row must have every column, or the file is not a rectangle.
hints: The columns aren't a fixed list you can type into the script — they have to be read off the data itself, once, before you build a single row. Get that list first; building it row by row as you go is how two students end up with columns in a different order.

`groupBy` gets you one bucket of records per student. For each bucket, don't just turn the records you have into columns — walk the full discovered list of subjects and look up a score for each one, so a student misses a subject rather than the subject disappearing from their row.

`(payload map $.subject) distinctBy $` gives the subjects in first-seen order — `distinctBy` keeps the first match, so that order is stable no matter which student saw a subject first. Then `reduce` over that same list, once per student, building `{ student: ... }` up one column at a time, defaulting a missing lookup to `0` rather than leaving the key out.
solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/csv
var subjects = (payload map $.subject) distinctBy $
---
payload groupBy $.student pluck ((rows, student) -> subjects reduce ((subj, acc = { student: student }) -> acc ++ { (subj): (rows filter ($.subject == subj))[0].score default 0 }))

mustFail.why: hardcodes the sample answer's exact CSV text
mustFail.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/csv
---
[{student: "Ada", Math: 90, Bio: 70}, {student: "Bo", Math: 60, Bio: 0}]

mustFail.why: builds each row only from the subjects that student actually has, instead of the full discovered list, so a student missing a subject produces a row with fewer columns than the others and the CSV comes out ragged
mustFail.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/csv
---
payload groupBy $.student pluck ((rows, student) -> rows reduce ((r, acc = {student: student}) -> acc ++ {(r.subject): r.score}))

explanation.approach: The set of output columns is not known until the whole input has been looked at, so it has to be computed once, up front, rather than assembled row by row. `(payload map $.subject) distinctBy $` collects every subject exactly once, in the order it first shows up, and `distinctBy` keeping the first match is what makes that order the same regardless of which student happens to mention a subject first. From there, `groupBy $.student` buckets the records per student, and for each bucket a `reduce` over the full subject list — not over that student's own rows — builds one row with a key for every column, filling in `0` wherever that student has no matching record. Reducing over the student's own rows instead of the discovered list is the natural-looking mistake: it works until two students have different subjects, at which point the rows stop having the same columns.

snippets.label: Discovering the columns, in first-seen order
snippets.note: Math and Bio, each once, in the order they first appear — Bo's second Math record does not add a duplicate or move anything.

snippets.label: groupBy buckets by student; the row is built by reduce over the SUBJECT list
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
var subjects = (payload map $.subject) distinctBy $
---
payload groupBy $.student pluck ((rows, student) -> subjects reduce ((subj, acc = { student: student }) -> acc ++ { (subj): (rows filter ($.subject == subj))[0].score default 0 }))
snippets.note: Bo never sat Bio, so filtering his rows for subject Bio finds nothing, `[0]` on that empty array is null, `.score` on null is null, and `default 0` turns that into the column value. Bo's row still has a Bio key.

snippets.label: The same result written out as the CSV the question actually asks for

snippets.note: Every row has exactly three fields in the same order, so the CSV writer's header lines up with every row underneath it.

snippets.label: The near-miss: reducing over a student's OWN rows instead of the full subject list
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/csv
---
payload groupBy $.student pluck ((rows, student) -> rows reduce ((r, acc = {student: student}) -> acc ++ {(r.subject): r.score}))
snippets.note: This compiles, runs, and looks right for Ada. Bo only ever appears with a Math record, so his row only ever gets a Math key — the writer takes its header from the first row (Ada's, with Bio) and then writes Bo's shorter row underneath it misaligned, one column short, instead of erroring.

snippets.label: A subject discovered late still becomes a column for the students seen earlier
snippets.script:

snippets.label: A record with no score at all still produces a column, filled with 0
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/csv
var subjects = (payload map $.subject) distinctBy $
---
payload groupBy $.student pluck ((rows, student) -> subjects reduce ((subj, acc = { student: student }) -> acc ++ { (subj): (rows filter ($.subject == subj))[0].score default 0 }))
snippets.note: Cy's record has a subject but no score field. `.score` on that record is null, same as a subject with no record at all, so `default 0` covers both a missing row and a missing field with the same fallback.
